title: The Rugby World Cup at 40: How the Tournament Transformed the Game
summary: The Rugby World Cup began in 1987 as an experiment that many in the sport opposed. Four decades later it is rugby's defining event — the moment every player builds their career around. We look at how it changed everything.
content:
When the first Rugby World Cup was held in New Zealand and Australia in 1987, the sport was still amateur. Players held day jobs. Training was fitted around work schedules. The idea of a World Cup had been resisted for years by the game's administrators, who feared it would lead inevitably to professionalism and the death of the values that made rugby what it was.

They were right about the professionalism. They were wrong that it would destroy the game. The Rugby World Cup has made rugby union one of the world's most watched sports — and the professional era has produced a standard of play that the amateur game could never have achieved.

The Early Years

New Zealand won the first two World Cups, in 1987 and then — after Australia's triumph in 1991 — the dominance of the southern hemisphere was established early. South Africa, returning from isolation in 1995, won on home soil in one of sport's most politically charged moments. Nelson Mandela wearing a Springbok jersey and presenting the trophy to Francois Pienaar remains one of the most iconic images in sporting history.

Australia won again in 1999. England, in 2003, became the first northern hemisphere nation to win the tournament — Jonny Wilkinson's extra-time drop goal against Australia in Sydney is one of the most replayed moments in rugby history. The drama, the precision, the weight of the moment — it was everything a World Cup final should be.

"I just kept telling myself: hit it cleanly, hit it truly. Everything else was noise." — Jonny Wilkinson on his 2003 World Cup winning drop goal

The All Blacks and Their Demons

No story in Rugby World Cup history is more compelling than New Zealand's relationship with the tournament. The All Blacks have been the world's best team for most of the professional era — their win rate is extraordinary, their playing style influential, their culture the envy of every other rugby nation. And yet they went 24 years between World Cup victories, from 1987 to 2011.

That gap — the expectation, the near-misses, the quarterfinale exits that shocked the world — defined New Zealand rugby for a generation. When they finally won in 2011, on home soil, the relief was palpable. When they won again in 2015, they became the first team to retain the trophy. The demons were gone.

What the Tournament Has Become

The Rugby World Cup is now one of the biggest sporting events on earth. The 2019 tournament in Japan — the first in Asia — drew record global audiences and introduced the sport to millions of new fans. The host nation's passionate support for the tournament helped make it one of the most celebrated editions in the event's history.

Ticket demand, television rights, sponsorship — all have grown to a scale that the amateur administrators of 1987 could not have imagined. The World Cup made rugby global. And the game, for all its changes, remains what it has always been: a contest of physical courage, tactical intelligence, and collective will that no other sport quite replicates.
